plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single ray diagram of image formation by a converging lens. A biconvex lens, shaded pale blue with a vertical dashed line through its center, stands upright on a horizontal optical axis. A red upward arrow to the left of the lens is the object, and its height is marked h_o by a double-headed arrow at the far left edge. Two red dots on the axis mark the focal points, each labeled F, one on either side of the lens, and a bracket from the lens center to the right-hand focal point is labeled f. Three rays leave the tip of the object. Ray 1, in red, travels parallel to the axis and bends at the lens to pass through the far focal point. Ray 2, in green, runs straight through the center without deviation. Ray 3, in purple, passes through the near focal point before emerging parallel to the axis. The three rays cross below the axis on the right, where a short red downward arrow of height h_i marks the inverted image. Horizontal brackets beneath the axis give the object distance d_o and the image distance d_i. Because each ray follows a different simple rule, their common crossing point fixes the position and size of the image by drawing alone, and the image produced here is one that could be caught on a screen.

interactionPlan.concept: Three principal rays, each obeying one simple drawing rule, intersect at a single point that fixes the image's position and size, and that intersection moves exactly as the thin-lens equation predicts when the object distance changes.
elements: horizontal optical axis line spanning the figure
biconvex converging lens, pale blue fill, centered on the axis with a vertical dashed centerline
object: red upward arrow standing on the axis to the left of the lens
object-height marker h_o: vertical double-headed arrow at the far left edge
two focal points: red dots on the axis, one each side of the lens, each labeled F
focal-length bracket f: horizontal double-headed bracket from lens center to the right focal point
ray 1 (red): leaves object tip parallel to the axis, refracts at the lens to pass through the far (right) focal point, labeled '1'
ray 2 (green): leaves object tip and passes straight through the lens center undeviated, labeled '2'
ray 3 (purple): leaves object tip through the near (left) focal point, refracts at the lens to emerge parallel to the axis, labeled '3'
image: red downward (inverted) arrow on the axis to the right where the three rays cross
image-height marker h_i: vertical double-headed arrow beside the image arrow
object-distance bracket d_o: horizontal double-headed bracket beneath the axis from object to lens center
image-distance bracket d_i: horizontal double-headed bracket beneath the axis from lens center to image

interactions.label: Object distance d_o
interactions.teaches: Dragging the object toward or away from the lens makes all three rays redraw and the image shift and resize: as d_o decreases toward f, d_i grows and the inverted image enlarges, making the 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f tradeoff visible by eye

Selecting ray 1, 2, or 3 highlights that ray's single construction rule (parallel-to-axis then through far F; straight through the center; through near F then parallel) and its associated focal/center marker, showing that three independent easy-to-draw rules nonetheless converge on the very same image point

interactions.label: Overlay
interactions.teaches: Switching on the measurement brackets attaches the quantities f, d_o, d_i, h_o, h_i to the moving rays and image, connecting the geometric construction to the magnification m = -d_i/d_o = h_i/h_o and the thin-lens equation

demo_steps.title: Three rules, one crossing
demo_steps.narration: Each colored ray follows a different simple rule, yet all three meet at a single point below the axis on the right — that crossing is the inverted real image, located purely by drawing.

demo_steps.title: Inspect each ray's rule
demo_steps.narration: Click ray 1, then 2, then 3 to see the one rule each uses (parallel-then-focal, undeviated center, focal-then-parallel) and notice that despite their different paths they still agree on the same image point.

demo_steps.title: Move the object
demo_steps.narration: Drag the d_o slider: as the object approaches the focal point the image recedes and grows (still inverted); as it moves far away the image shrinks toward the focal plane — the lens-equation tradeoff made visible.

demo_steps.title: Read off the equation
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the measurement overlay so the brackets f, d_o, d_i, h_o, h_i track the moving figure; the ratios you see are exactly m = -d_i/d_o = h_i/h_o and 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The image is not drawn by guesswork: three independent, trivially-constructible ray rules intersect at one point, and that intersection is precisely the position and magnification the thin-lens equation computes.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Horizontal optical axis across the middle; a tall pale-blue biconvex lens centered on it with a vertical dashed centerline. Red upward object arrow on the left with an h_o double-headed marker at the far-left edge. Two red focal dots labeled F symmetric about the lens, with an f bracket from center to the right F. Ray 1 red (horizontal to lens, then through right F), ray 2 green (straight through center), ray 3 purple (through left F, then horizontal after the lens), each with a small numeric label near its first segment and arrowheads along its path. The three rays cross below the axis on the right at the tip of a short red downward image arrow, with an h_i marker beside it. Beneath the axis, d_o and d_i double-headed brackets. Keep red/green/purple color coding consistent; when a ray is clicked, thicken/brighten it and emphasize its focal or center marker while dimming the others; measurement brackets fade in/out on toggle and must reposition live as the d_o slider moves the object, rays, and image together.

authoredContext:
Consider an object some distance away from a converging lens, as shown in the figure. To find the location and size of the image, we trace the paths of selected light rays originating from one point on the object, in this case, the tip of the arrow. The figure shows three rays from many rays that emanate from the tip of the arrow. These three rays can be traced by using the ray-tracing rules given above.

Several important distances appear in the figure. As for a mirror, we define do to be the object distance, or the distance of an object from the center of a lens. The image distance di is defined to be the distance of the image from the center of a lens. The height of the object and the height of the image are indicated by ho and hi, respectively. Images that appear upright relative to the object have positive heights, and those that are inverted have negative heights. By using the rules of ray tracing and making a scale drawing with paper and pencil, like that in the figure, we can accurately describe the location and size of an image. But the real benefit of ray tracing is in visualizing how images are formed in a variety of situations.

Although three rays are traced in this figure, only two are necessary to locate a point of the image. It is best to trace rays for which there are simple ray-tracing rules.

Ray tracing is used to locate the image formed by a lens. Rays originating from the same point on the object are traced—the three chosen rays each follow one of the rules for ray tracing, so that their paths are easy to determine. The image is located at the point where the rays cross. In this case, a real image—one that can be projected on a screen—is formed.

Figure shows the cross section of a bi-convex lens. Three rays originate from the top of an object and enter the lens. Ray 1 is parallel to the optical axis. Ray 2 crosses the center of the lens. Ray 3 crosses the focal point in front of the lens. All rays converge on the other side at the top of an inverted image. Ray 1 crosses the focal point behind the lens. Ray 2 is undeviated. Ray 3 becomes parallel to the optical axis. The object distance and image distances are d subscript o and d subscript I respectively. The object and image heights are h subscript o and h subscript I respectively. The focal length is f.
